title: The conflict alert that never fired
intro: A separation monitor watches pairs of flight paths and alerts when they come too close. Two aircraft passed within a third of the required minimum and nothing fired. Open the clues.

facts.label: The event
facts.value: Recorded tracks show the pair closed to well under the separation minimum. No alert was raised at any point.

facts.label: The monitor
facts.value: For each pair it solves for an intersection point of the two paths. If a solution exists, it computes the time to that point and alerts when the time is short.

facts.label: The geometry
facts.value: The two paths are skew: neither parallel nor intersecting. The solver correctly reports that no intersection point exists.

facts.label: The altitudes
facts.value: The aircraft were on crossing headings at different, closely spaced flight levels.

facts.label: The arithmetic
facts.value: The intersection solver was validated against dozens of crossing-at-the-same-level cases and is exact on every one.

facts.label: The alert log
facts.value: No error, no exception, no 'no solution' warning. The pair was simply evaluated and passed over.

composition.label: A 2-D test applied to a 3-D problem

question: What actually failed?
choices: The intersection solver has a numerical tolerance that missed a near-intersection
The monitor asks whether the paths INTERSECT, but skew paths never intersect — in three dimensions the right question is the shortest distance between them, which it never computes
The altitude data was missing from the track records
The separation minimum was configured too low
debrief:
The solver is correct and the geometry is correct. In three dimensions, two paths that are neither parallel nor intersecting are **skew**, and skew lines genuinely have no intersection point — so a monitor built around 'do they intersect?' has nothing to report, and says nothing.

The right question is the **shortest distance** `d = |(a₂ − a₁) · (b₁ × b₂)| / |b₁ × b₂|`, with an alert when d falls below the separation minimum. That number exists for every pair of non-parallel lines, including the ones that never meet, which is exactly why it is the one to threshold on.

The clue that explains how this survived testing is the quiet one: the solver was validated against **crossing-at-the-same-level** cases — all of which genuinely intersect. A test suite built entirely from the intersecting case cannot discover that the skew case is unhandled. That is a 2-D intuition baked into a 3-D system, and the coplanar test data preserved it.

The broader move: when a model has a case that only appears in higher dimensions, the fixtures have to include it deliberately. Nothing in the lower-dimensional data will ever produce it.
